Well, I've been farming these 6.5 mu for over 40 years now — since I was 18. My father taught me, and I've figured out what works and what doesn't on this particular soil. I'm 61, not as strong as I used to be, but I know every corner of these fields. My wife helps me, and my son works in a factory over in Shijiazhuang. He sends some money home, which helps with my granddaughter's school fees, but farming is still our base. I have to watch every yuan.

It's October now. Just finished harvesting the summer maize last week — got about 460 jin per mu, decent but not great, August was too dry. The chili is done too, picked the last batch ten days ago. Now the rush is getting the winter wheat in the ground. The soil is dry, so I'll run the pump for a day to wet it down, then till and plant. I aim for around October 12th. The neighbors are planting around the same time, so the weather's about right.

I've got 5 mu in wheat-maize double crop — that's my bread and butter, gives us grain to eat and some to sell. The other 1.5 mu I grow chili. Been doing that for about 12 years. It pays better than cotton most years, but the picking is back-breaking. My daughter-in-law helps when she can get away from her job in town, but if she's not around during the peak harvest in August and September, I hire Mrs. Wang from the next village for a few days.

**The wheat** — I plant Jinmai 47, been using it for six years now. It's reliable, doesn't fall over, and the grain station will buy it. Seed costs me about 35 yuan per mu, I buy fresh seed every two years. For fertilizer, the extension station fellow says I should use 15 kg nitrogen per mu, but last year I used about 13 kg and got 420 kg per mu, which is plenty for me. I put down about 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base — that's what I can afford. Then at green-up in March I spread about 8 kg of urea per mu, and another 7 kg or so at jointing in April. Total nitrogen is maybe 13 kg per mu. I don't calculate it exactly — I go by the scoop and what my pocket allows.

I'll irrigate three times: once before winter if it stays dry, once in late March at green-up, and once in early May at grain filling. The electricity for the pump costs about 12 yuan per mu each time now. Three times is enough — Old Zhang down the road does four, but he's got a bigger farm and more cash. For weeds, I spray herbicide once after planting, about 15 yuan per mu. I don't usually spray insecticide on wheat unless I see armyworms.

**The maize** — I plant Jinchan 58 hybrid right after wheat harvest, usually June 10th or 11th. The window is tight, maybe five days, so I don't deep till — no time. Minimal tillage with my small tractor and plant. Seed costs about 45 yuan per mu for the hybrid. I put down about 35 kg of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, then side-dress with about 10 kg of urea when the maize is knee-high. Total nitrogen is about 12 kg per mu. I irrigate twice if the rains don't come — once at the 7-leaf stage, and maybe once at tasseling. Pumping costs add up, so I watch the sky. I'll spray herbicide once and maybe insecticide if I see borers.

**The chili** — I plant that in late April on the 1.5 mu plot. I buy seedlings from the market in Quzhou town, about 50 yuan per mu. It's an improved local variety, good for drying and the spice buyer comes right to the village. I plough that plot with my walking tractor and make ridges — chili hates wet feet. I put about 25 kg of compound fertilizer down before transplanting, then topdress with a bit of urea and some potassium fertilizer when it flowers. Total nitrogen maybe 8 kg per mu. Chili needs more pesticide than grain — I spray for aphids about three times and fungicide twice for that black spot disease. Chemicals run about 40 yuan per mu. I irrigate three times.

Labor is always tight. For wheat and maize, my wife and I manage most of it — planting, fertilizing, irrigating, hauling the grain home. The combine does the cutting but we still dry and bag it ourselves. That's about 10 days of work for wheat and 8 for maize. The chili is another story — between transplanting, managing, and picking over four months, it's maybe 22 days of our labor. If my daughter-in-law can't get time off during the main picking in August, I hire Mrs. Wang for 5 days at 100 yuan per day. She's getting older too, so I pay her fairly.

My total input costs this year will run about 2,100 yuan. That's a lot for a farm my size, but I can't cut much more without risking a bad year. I'd rather spend a bit more on fertilizer than risk losing half my yield — a bad year hurts more than a good year helps, I've learned that the hard way. My son's remittances mean I don't have to choose between fertilizer and my granddaughter's schoolbooks, but I still sleep better knowing I have some cash in the jar for emergencies.

I expect about 420 kg per mu of wheat, 480 kg per mu of maize, and about 300 kg per mu of fresh chili. Not pushing for records — at my age, stable and decent is good enough.
